strengths: The construction connects learned discriminative partitions with class-conditional Gaussian mixtures in an understandable way. Researchers in density estimation, uncertainty estimation, and small-sample classification form an identifiable interested audience. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b10/review-experiment-70_lc_cp/call-d7cbce1050674958ad60b816ea7eb88f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The five synthetic problems, sample-size sweeps, and 45 repetitions provide useful evidence about the methods' behavior. Posterior visualizations complement classification and OOD metrics, and Table 1 reports substantial AUROC improvements over the parent classifiers on the tested exterior-region distributions.

With nonsingular covariance matrices, the unmodified density estimates are normalized Gaussian mixtures that support sampling. Adding a common positive bias also provides a transparent mechanism for returning predictions toward empirical class priors far from the training data.
The experiment with 126 retained human participants provides an interesting behavioral observation. Reporting recruitment and exclusion criteria helps readers interpret this exploratory component.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central theoretical claims are not established, constituting a substantive failure of the evidence criterion. In Theorem 1, counts in partitions learned from the same observations are not generally binomial with fixed cell probabilities. A shrinking Gaussian does not become uniform within its cell, so the asserted E[K_s(x)] approaching 1/h_s is unjustified. Vanishing covariance terms and contributions from other cells are also asserted without adequate bounds. Even a valid asymptotic-unbiasedness result would not establish the introduction's convergence claims, and no result establishes the abstract's theoretical efficiency advantage. Provide a valid analysis for the actual estimators or withdraw these claims.

Necessary: Clarify the probabilistic interpretation and scope of the OOD result. On R^d, adding a positive constant makes the density in Eq. (3.6) nonintegrable. Equation (3.8) remains a normalized classification rule, but its inputs are no longer class-conditional probability densities. Its far-distance limit is the empirical class prior, which is uniform only for balanced classes. This limit does not establish the goal in Eq. (2.1) for all support-disjoint OOD distributions, particularly near the training support. Separate the normalized generative model from the biased classification scores and narrow the robustness claims accordingly.

Necessary: Resolve consequential ambiguities in the estimator. The manuscript does not give values or selection procedures for h, T, and C, or explain how singular covariance estimates are handled in sparsely populated polytopes. Equation (3.4) measures pre-activation differences, whereas Algorithm 3 accumulates post-activation differences; these define different weighting rules. These omissions prevent readers from implementing and assessing the reported method reliably.

Necessary: Correct and complete the experimental specification. As written, Gaussian XOR assigns identical mixture distributions to both classes, implying chance-level Bayes accuracy and contradicting the results. The treatment of Gaussian tails when restricting samples to the square also needs specification. Explain the held-out evaluation protocol, OOD sampling distribution, computation of true posteriors and Hellinger distances, and meaning of Table 1's uncertainty values. Its caption incorrectly calls FPR@95 a false-negative rate.

Necessary: Align the performance claims with Figure 2. KDF has appreciably worse small-sample classification error than RF on Circle, and both kernel variants have worse small-sample Hellinger distance than their parents on Gaussian XOR. These results contradict claims of always obtaining closer posteriors and avoiding any sacrifice in in-distribution performance. Table 1 also reports FPR@95 values around 0.28–0.41 despite high AUROC. The abstract, experimental discussion, and conclusion should describe these tradeoffs and limit conclusions to the evaluated settings.

Necessary: The human-similarity claim exceeds the presented analysis. Figure 3 compares humans with RF and DN, without directly evaluating KDF or KDN, and emphasizes one 82-degree slice of the Spiral task without uncertainty estimates or quantitative model–human comparisons. An average response near 0.5 does not distinguish individual uncertainty from disagreement among confident participants. Provide analyses supporting the claimed similarity or restrict the conclusion to the observed aggregate human responses.

Optional: Comparisons with ordinary KDE or Gaussian mixtures using the same bias, together with weighting ablations, would help identify what the learned partitions contribute. Consolidating the duplicated appendix pseudocode and filling or removing the empty Algorithm 5 would improve presentation. Broader benchmarks could extend the contribution, but are not prerequisites for a sound paper with an explicitly low-dimensional scope.
